description: Long before rockets, people looked up and wondered: what if we could go there? We are The Syndicate, five friends from Hanoi who never stopped asking. Our mission is to turn that wonder into a game anyone can play: pick a destination, design your spacecraft, and make hard choices about fuel, budget and risk. You will laugh, fail, try again, and learn how real missions come to life. Five people, one dream.
summary: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. For students who rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation, these trade-offs often remain abstract. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?SOL-15: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 3D browser-based space survival simulator designed specifically for students ages 7–12. Players step into the role of an Outpost Commander managing a lunar or Martian base over a simulated 15-day mission to protect Junior Astronaut An and launch the return ship to Earth.

  • Pre-Flight Payload Triage: Before landing, players configure essential scientific modules (such as the Kilopower nuclear reactor, Sabatier water recovery unit, and Spirulina algae tanks) within a strict 15-ton lander mass limit.
  • Real-Time Resource Management (ECLSS): Using intuitive HUD sliders, players balance power across five core subsystems: Oxygen & Thermal Control, Hydroponics Biodome, Regolith Radiation Shielding, Water Walls, and ISRU Ice Mining / Fuel Synthesis.
  • Dual Planetary Environments: With a single click, players can switch between the Moon (Artemis Shackleton Crater)—enduring -173°C lunar nights and mining water ice—and Mars—tracking time in Sols, surviving global dust storms, and extracting Oxygen from atmospheric CO2 using NASA's MOXIE technology.
  • Emergency Drills & Day-15 Launch: Players must react to dynamic space weather alerts (Solar Particle Events, system malfunctions) and maintain Oxygen $\ge 40\%$, Food $\ge 30\%$, and 100% rocket fuel to safely launch Junior Astronaut An home on Day 15.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Bridges the STEM Translation Gap: Translates complex NASA aerospace engineering and life-support physics into tangible, visual gameplay that holds the attention of young learners without dumbing down the science.
  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Runs directly in any modern web browser with no downloads, installations, or account sign-ups required, making it ideal for classrooms, parents, and judges.
  • Develops Systems Thinking: Trains students in critical thinking, long-term planning, and crisis management under strict resource constraints.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?

  • Inspiring the Next Generation of Explorers: Empowers kids ages 7–12 to think like real NASA mission planners and sparks early interest in aerospace engineering, planetary science, and sustainability.
  • Connecting Space Tech to Earth Sustainability: Through a post-mission analytical debrief, players learn how closed-loop space technologies directly solve challenges on Earth—such as using 98% Sabatier water recycling for drought-stricken regions, low-water LED hydroponics for urban agriculture, and resilient microgrids for renewable energy.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • 3D Graphics & Shaders: Three.js (r128), WebGL, PMREM environment reflection mapping, particle weather systems, and custom GLSL Shaders for atmospheric scattering and hexagonal radiation-shielding water walls.
  • Frontend & Data Visualization: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, and HTML5 Canvas for real-time telemetry graphs.
  • Audio Synthesis: Web Audio API to procedurally generate cockpit alerts and ambient soundscapes without external audio files.
  • Physics & Math Engine: Custom JavaScript differential equations modeling mass-energy balance, thermal thermodynamics, and cumulative radiation exposure based on NASA baselines.
  • AI Assistance: Google Gemini was utilized to assist with Three.js/WebGL code optimization, mathematical modeling from NASA open datasets, UI/UX layout, and documentation.

5. How is your project creative?

  • "No Choice Is Free" Trade-Off Mechanics: Instead of simple "safe" upgrades, every action carries a realistic engineering consequence—for instance, deploying 90% Regolith Shielding and Water Walls blocks up to 92% of deadly solar radiation, but simultaneously cuts solar panel output and restricts water availability for crops.
  • 100% Procedural Assets: All 3D outpost structures, PBR surface textures, and cockpit sound effects are generated purely through mathematical code, resulting in an ultra-lightweight, instant-loading web application.
  • Dual-World Instant Switching: Seamlessly contrasts lunar and Martian physics in one unified training simulator, encouraging high replayability and experimentation.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Age-Appropriate Accessibility (Ages 7–12): Replaced dense technical jargon with color-coded telemetry, clear icons, and relatable storytelling centered around rescuing Junior Astronaut An, while retaining authentic NASA math underneath.
  • Scientific Authenticity: Grounded all resource consumption rates (e.g., 0.84 kg O2/person/day), radiation thresholds (100 mSv limit), and environmental parameters directly in official NASA open datasets (DONKI, OSDR, BVAD TP-2015-218570, MOXIE, and Kilopower).
  • Replayability & Constructive Failure: Designed randomized space weather events and pre-flight payload choices so every playthrough offers a new scenario, treating mission failures as non-punitive learning opportunities.
